extracted.intended_audience: research funders, peer review methodologists, science policy researchers, and funding-agency staff who design or evaluate grant review processes
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and comparison of two methods (rating vs ranking) for peer review of research grant applications, including the specific criteria used in CIHR Foundation competitions, scoring mechanics, reliability metrics, and predictors of bias and variance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment method — Rating (absolute judgment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most funding agencies ask reviewers to rate an application on an ordinal scale from poor to excellent (absolute judgment) for individual criteria and an overall application score; requires a reviewer to judge against an internalized concept of an 'ideal' application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absolute judgment depends on reviewer experience (experienced reviewers have more stable concept of 'ideal') and is more sensitive to differences in reviewer harshness/leniency; observed lower reliability than ranking (phase 1 ICC = 0.54; phase 2 ICC = 0.25). Rating showed sex bias at lower H-index values and was more susceptible to reviewer characteristics (experience, domain-match, expertise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment method — Ranking (relative judgment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers rank applications from highest quality to lowest (relative judgment) rather than scoring against an internal ideal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expected to be more reliable and less sensitive to reviewer expertise/experience and leniency. In this study ranking was more reliable than rating (phase 1 ICC = 0.59; phase 2 ICC = 0.38), reduced some sources of bias (sex bias less evident), and forced tie-breaking which helped distinguish applications. Rankings were standardized to percentiles and averaged across reviewers to produce final scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase 1 evaluation criteria — vision
rubrics_metrics.description: One of four criteria used in Phase 1 to assess the caliber of the applicant: vision (assessed from CV and a two-page summary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rated using letter grades then converted to numeric scores; showed relatively low inter-rater agreement (ICC for vision = 0.35 in phase 1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase 1 evaluation criteria — impact
rubrics_metrics.description: One of four criteria used in Phase 1 to assess the caliber of the applicant: impact (assessed from CV and a two-page summary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rated with letter grades converted to numeric scores and incorporated into the overall applicant score and ranking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase 1 evaluation criteria — productivity
rubrics_metrics.description: One of four Phase 1 criteria assessing applicant productivity (assessed from CV and a two-page summary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Had the highest ICC among phase 1 criteria (ICC = 0.50), indicating relatively better agreement among reviewers on productivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase 1 evaluation criteria — leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: One of four Phase 1 criteria assessing applicant leadership (assessed from CV and a two-page summary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Among the highest scoring criteria in phase 1 (mean 21.9 out of 28 for that item).

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase 2 evaluation criteria — research concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Phase 2 criterion assessing the quality of the research concept for the program of research (assessed from a 10-page application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Together with research approach, contributed to 50% of the phase 2 weighted score; reliability for project-related criteria was lower than for applicant criteria (phase 2 reliability overall lower).

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase 2 evaluation criteria — research approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Phase 2 criterion assessing the research approach for the program of research (assessed from a 10-page application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weighted heavily (part of the 50% combined weight with research concept); among phase 2 criteria reliability was highest for research approach (ICC = 0.23) though still low.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase 2 evaluation criteria — expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Phase 2 criterion assessing the expertise of the applicant/team relevant to the program of research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the 40% weight with mentorship; reviewers graded this with the same letter-to-score conversion; proportion of reviewers with high expertise was associated with higher scores and reduced variance in phase 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase 2 evaluation criteria — mentorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Phase 2 criterion assessing mentorship aspects of the program of research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combined with expertise to form 40% of the weighted phase 2 score; evaluated via letter grades converted to numeric values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase 2 evaluation criteria — environmental support
rubrics_metrics.description: Phase 2 criterion assessing the environmental support available for the research program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocated 10% of phase 2 weight; had among the lowest reliability in phase 2 (support ICC = 0.12).

rubrics_metrics.name: Letter-grade scoring scale and numeric conversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers graded individual criteria using letter grades (poor, fair, good, excellent, excellent+, excellent++, outstanding, outstanding+, outstanding++). Letter grades were converted to numeric scores (phase 1: 0 to 28 per criterion, max 112; phase 2: max 140).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Converted numeric scores were used to establish preliminary rank order; reviewers then adjusted ranks and ties were eliminated where applicable. The mapping and range influence granularity of rating and tie frequency (tie-breaking was common).

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase 2 criterion weighting schema
rubrics_metrics.description: In Phase 2 the criteria were weighted differently: 50% weight to research concept and approach, 40% to expertise and mentoring, and 10% to environmental support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weighting affects overall numeric scores and relative influence of each criterion on final rankings and scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rank standardization to percentiles and aggregation
rubrics_metrics.description: Because reviewers rated differing numbers of applications, ranks were standardized by converting them to percentiles. The mean of all reviewers’ percentile ranks was used as the final score for an application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Percentile conversion allows aggregation across reviewers with different assignment sizes but can add noise (e.g., a given ordinal rank maps to different percentiles depending on the number of applications the reviewer had), slightly reducing ICC; unequal reviewer workload/distribution of application quality can introduce measurement error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tie-breaking and reviewer-adjusted ranks
rubrics_metrics.description: After converting letter grades to numeric scores and establishing a preliminary rank order, reviewers adjusted the application rank to reflect best-to-worst and to eliminate ties when applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tie-breaking forced reviewers to reflect on nuanced differences and likely increased between-application variance, improving reliability of ranking relative to pure scoring; many reviewers had to break ties (84% in phase 1 had at least one tie).

rubrics_metrics.name: Flagging for asynchronous (online) discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications were flagged for asynchronous discussion if there were differences in scores and ranks greater than one standard deviation, or if the virtual chair identified comments/questions warranting discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Online discussion was associated with increased rater variance (marker of disagreement) but also with higher final scores and ranks for discussed applications; used as a process control to resolve divergent opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability metric — intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC)
rubrics_metrics.description: ICC was used to estimate reliability of overall rating and percentile ranking scores and of individual criterion ratings; bootstrapping used for 95% CIs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported ICCs indicate ranking > rating overall (phase 1: rating 0.54 vs ranking 0.59; phase 2: rating 0.25 vs ranking 0.38). Individual criterion ICCs vary widely (e.g., productivity higher, vision lower).

rubrics_metrics.name: Within-rater variance (log) as an outcome measure of agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Between-rater variance for an application was calculated and the log of this variance was used as the outcome variable to assess predictors of reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used generalized estimating equation multiple linear regression (accounting for clustering of applications within applicants) to estimate associations between characteristics (applicant, reviewer, application) and rater variance for rating and ranking methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of H-index as proxy for applicant scientific productivity/quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal applicant’s H-index was used as a measure of scientific productivity and as a proxy for application quality in models assessing bias and reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: H-index strongly associated with final application score and rank; quadratic term tested due to non-linear relationship; interaction terms (H-index*sex, H-index*age) used to detect effect modification (e.g., sex differences at lower H-index values).

rubrics_metrics.name: Early career investigator classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants were classified as early career investigators if the application was submitted within 5 years of their first university/institute research appointment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early career investigators received lower scores and ranks in both phase 1 and 2 (penalized), although effects were less pronounced for ranking vs rating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count of unique collaborators and adjustment for collaborator bias on H-index
rubrics_metrics.description: Because H-index can be positively biased by number of collaborators, the number of unique collaborators on an applicant's publications was also counted and included in analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an additional covariate to account for inflation of H-index due to large collaboration networks; included in multivariate models assessing bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer experience (years since 2000)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer experience measured as mean number of years of review experience since 2000 for reviewers assigned to an application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greater reviewer experience was associated with reduced rater variance for rating but had little influence on ranking, consistent with theory that experience stabilizes absolute judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion of reviewers self-reporting high expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: For each application, the proportion of reviewers who self-assessed as having high expertise to review that application was measured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher proportion of high-expertise reviewers was associated with reduced variance and higher scores/ranks in phase 2; expertise proportion influenced rating more than ranking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion of reviewers whose prior applications were in the same scientific domain
rubrics_metrics.description: Measured proportion of reviewers whose prior applications were in the same scientific domain as the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A greater proportion in the same domain was associated with reduced rater variance for rating (e.g., -30.05% in phase 1), suggesting domain-match improves agreement for absolute scoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer workload — number of applications per reviewer
rubrics_metrics.description: Workload measured as the mean number of applications each reviewer was assigned to review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher reviewer workload was associated with increased rater variance and lower ratings (in phase 1); number of applications per reviewer influenced rating but not ranking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer sex mix
rubrics_metrics.description: The sex composition of reviewers assigned to an application (sex mix) was measured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Female reviewers tend to score systematically lower than male reviewers in prior literature; sex mix did not significantly influence overall score/rank here, but sex of applicant interacted with H-index in rating models (female applicants with low H-index rated lower).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicts of interest proportion among invited reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportion of reviewers who declined to review an application because of conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of conflicts on a panel was associated with higher application scores and ranks (even when conflicted reviewers did not score or discuss), possibly indicating conflicts as a marker of applicant prominence or network; note this differs from assumptions about cronyism in in-person panels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chair characteristics — number of reviewers responsible, number of applications assigned, chair review experience
rubrics_metrics.description: For each virtual chair: number of reviewers the chair was responsible for, number of applications the chair was assigned, and years of chair experience since 2000 were measured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These chair metrics influenced scores and variance (e.g., chairs responsible for more reviewers associated with higher ratings/ranks in phase 1); chairs may influence panel functioning and bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multivariate modeling and interaction testing to detect bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Two multivariate models were created (one with overall mean rating as outcome, one with mean percentile ranking) including H-index, log number of collaborators, applicant, application and review characteristics, and interaction terms (H-index*applicant sex, H-index*applicant age) to test effect modification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This modelling approach allowed assessment of systematic bias (e.g., sex or age effects among applicants with equivalent productivity) and revealed that sex bias was evident for rating at lower H-index values but not for ranking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of percentile ranks and ties as a mechanism to force discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Because many reviewers produced tied numeric scores, reviewers were required to break ties and the resulting ranks were converted to percentiles to combine across reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tie-breaking compelled reviewers to make relative distinctions that improved discrimination among applications and likely improved reliability of ranking compared to raw numeric rating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveats about unequal distribution of application quality between reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Unequal distribution of the quality of applications assigned to each reviewer (and unequal numbers of applications reviewed) can introduce noise in percentile conversions and measurement error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Future ranking implementations should aim for more equitable assignment sizes and distribution to maximize reliability; unequal assignments partially explain why percentile conversion reduced ICC slightly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observed systematic effects — age and early-career status
rubrics_metrics.description: Older applicants received higher scores and ranks (phase 1) and early career investigators received lower scores and ranks in both phases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both rating and ranking penalized early career investigators and favored older applicants; ranking reduced but did not eliminate these effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observed sex bias pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Sex bias was evident only for rating and only when the applicant’s H-index was at the lower end of the distribution — female applicants with low H-index were rated lower than male counterparts; at high H-index female applicants were rated equivalently or better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ranking attenuated this sex bias; implication: relative judgments may reduce some systematic biases inherent in absolute ratings.
